Summary (auto): quick POC sync to review throughput numbers from last 48h, adjust continuous batching parameters, discuss concurrency ceilings and queueing behavior, and agree on an overnight stress test. Action items captured at end.

Topics:
- 48h run results (p50/p95 latencies, tokens/sec, cost)

- Concurrency targets and backpressure/queueing

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda—riya will walk through the 48 hour runs, then we'll talk tuning, and finish with next steps. sound good?
[00:12] Sara (BlueJar): yep, sounds good. Mark is on audio only but here.
[00:18] Riya (Redwood-SE): cool, i'll share my screen in a sec. bear with me, um, i'm pulling up the results spreadsheet, it's under redwood/poc/bluejar/results.csv — you should have access.
[00:27] Priya (BlueJar): got it. i see the CSV, thanks.
[00:33] Riya (Redwood-SE): ok so quick context — we ran two profiles: baseline (no continuous batching, concurrency target 8) and tuned (continuous batching enabled, max_batch_size 64, batch_timeout_ms 20, concurrency 16). runs each ~24 hours, steady-state traffic mimicked their production pattern.
[00:50] Mark (BlueJar): can i stop you — when you say batch_timeout, that's the window before a batch is flushed, right?
[00:55] Riya: yeah exactly, the ms window we wait to fill the batch. small note, transcription might show that as "bad timeout" in the csv so forgive the auto labels.
[01:03] Jordan: quick numbers first — baseline p50 token latency ~45ms per token, p95 ~210ms, throughput ~1.8k tokens/sec; tuned run p50 ~32ms, p95 ~160ms, throughput ~3.9k tokens/sec. cost per 1M tokens dropped ~18% due to better GPU utilization.
[01:25] Sara: that throughput bump looks great. what was variability across requests? are we seeing any big outliers?
[01:32] Riya: good question — the p99 stayed a bit high in tuned runs because of head-of-line blocking in our internal queue when concurrency spikes. you'll see periodic spikes when many short requests hit at once. that's where queueing/backpressure tuning comes in.
[01:45] Priya: can you explain head-of-line blocking briefly? i think i know but want to make sure we align.
[01:50] Riya: sure — if a large request gets into the front of the processing queue it can delay many small low-latency requests behind it, especially when we have a fixed number of worker slots. continuous batching helps amortize GPU overhead but doesn't eliminate queuing unless we shape the queue.
[02:08] Jordan: this is why we recommended request bucketing — small short requests should be routed to a low-latency lane (smaller batches, lower batch_timeout), while long requests go to the high-throughput lane. we can implement that in the delivery policy.
[02:22] Mark: is that something we need in the app gateway? or can redwood handle it on the runtime side?
[02:27] Riya: can do both — easiest path is at the runtime: route by token-length header. if you can set a request header from the gateway it's seamless. alternatively, LB-level routing by path is possible but more intrusive.
[02:42] Jordan: during the tuned run we tried runtime side and saw p50 for small-requests go to ~19ms and p95 ~90ms, so it's a margin improvement.
[02:52] Sara: curious about the concurrency number — you tested 16. is that the sweet spot?
[02:56] Riya: it's workload dependent. for your model (7B quantized variant) with average prompt length ~120 tokens, concurrency 16 gave best tokens/sec while keeping acceptable tail latency. we also tried 24, which increased throughput another 8% but p95 climbed close to 300ms — probably not acceptable for your interactive use-case.
[03:18] Priya: any guidance for autoscaling? we can't manually tune concurrency forever.
[03:22] Owen (Redwood): autoscaling should be driven by request queue length and observed p95. suggest target p95 < 200ms; scale up when queue length > 40 and scale down when queue < 8 for sustained 2 minutes. we can provide suggested HPA policies or a cloud-autoscaler hook.
[03:40] Mark: can you explain queue length metric — is that requests waiting on CPU before entering GPU?
[03:44] Riya: yes, it's the runtime's in-memory queue per worker-group; it counts inflight requests waiting to be batched/executed. we'll surface it as "runtime.queue.length" in the console.
[03:52] Jordan: quick interjection — we observed one weird failure in baseline: a surge caused LB upstream timeouts at 60s, which cascaded into retries. Mark, did you keep the gateway at default 60s?
[04:03] Mark: yes our nginx default is 60s. we can change it. what's redwood recommending?
[04:07] Riya: for interactive, lower your client-side timeout to 30s and ensure upstream idle timeouts are >120s on the worker side for long-running docs. also set connection pooling to reuse TCP connections to avoid TLS overhead.
[04:20] Priya: ok we'll try 30s.
[04:23] Sara: can you show me the run chart where p95 jumps?
[04:26] Riya: sharing chart — you should see here at ~03:12 UTC a spike in p95 — that's where a batch of long requests hit at once. you can see queue.length spike then GPU utilization goes to 98% and latency tails go up.
[04:42] Jordan: the mitigation path is threefold: 1) small-request lane 2) cap per-client concurrency (token buckets at gateway) 3) soft circuit-breaker that rejects or routes to a smaller faster model when backlog > threshold.
[04:58] Mark: about routing to a smaller model — what are the quality tradeoffs? is that something we can test?
[05:03] Riya: yes we suggested a 3B quantized variant as a fallback. in our eval it had slightly lower coherence on long-form but was fine for short Q&A. we can run a side-by-side quality regression using your eval prompts.
[05:15] Priya: add that to next steps.
[05:18] Jordan: noted.
[05:20] [05:20] Speaker noise / crosstalk (unlabeled): mm-hmm
[05:25] Riya: quick note on batching params we tuned: max_batch_size=64, batch_timeout_ms=20, batch_window_ms=5 (for pre-emptive micro-batching), continuous_batching=true. that config increased batch fill rate from 12% to 67% under your mix.
[05:42] Sara: can you explain batch_window?
[05:45] Riya: batch_window is an inner micro-window where we coalesce requests that arrive within very short intervals to avoid issuing too many tiny kernels; it helps with bursty traffic. it's especially useful when you have many short requests.
[05:57] Mark: are these values safe for our current GPU type? we're on T4s in the test cluster.
[06:02] Riya: yes T4s responded well, but quantized kernels saw higher throughput gains. we'll share kernel selection notes in the config doc; larger batch sizes can increase memory pressure so we'll call that out.
[06:15] Jordan: also important — KV cache behavior. if you have chat-like sessions where context re-use is high, we can enable prefix/KV caching to avoid re-tokenizing/pushing repeated context which reduces tokens/sec cost and latency. but there's memory tradeoff across sessions.
[06:30] Sara: we're 60% chat, 40% single-shot. so KV cache might help. what's the memory overhead?
[06:36] Riya: roughly linear with average seq length and number of cached sessions; for your numbers it looked like an extra ~6GB per 10k active sessions in our pilot topology. we can tune eviction and session TTLs.
[06:49] Priya: okay we need to bring this to infra folks — Mark, would you be able to evaluate mem/bandwidth?
[06:55] Mark: yes I'll run a back-of-envelope and put numbers in the ticket.
[07:00] Riya: returning to pressure/backpressure—we observed retries from client lib when we hit the concurrency cap. avoid aggressive client retries — prefer a 50-200ms jittered retry with exponential backoff and include retry-after header from our side.
[07:14] Jordan: we can emit retry-after values based on queue length thresholds.
[07:18] Sara: any logs we should look at? request traces?
[07:21] Riya: yes we captured traces and span-level timings — i'll share the console link: https://console.redwood.ai/poc/bluejar/traces (note: placeholder link in notes). logs include queue.enqueue_time, batch_fill_latency, kernel_exec_ms.
[07:35] Priya: can you attach the run CSV to the crm? makes it easier for execs.
[07:39] Jordan: done — uploading now to CRM and i'll send link in follow-up.
[07:44] Mark: one more question — you mentioned batching windows for prioritization; how do we do sudden priority promos (like admin alerts) without disrupting throughput?
[07:53] Riya: we support priority flags on requests — high-priority requests skip micro-batching and get a reserved slot; that slightly reduces overall throughput but keeps critical path low-latency. config flag per route.
[08:06] Sara: good. for SLAs we want p95 < 200ms for core flow and best-effort for analytics. can we produce daily SLO reports?
[08:15] Owen: yes, console can emit daily SLO reports and token-cost breakdowns per route — we'll enable retention for 30 days for the pilot.
[08:25] Priya: will that include cost by route?
[08:27] Owen: yes cost by token & per-call breakdown.
[08:30] Jordan: quick recap — tuned run looks promising, but tails need work. main mitigations: request bucketing into lanes, cap per-client concurrency, fallback model strategy, and LB/gateway timeout tuning. we'll do the overnight stress test at 3x peak tomorrow.
[08:47] Sara: what's the expected duration of the stress run?
[08:50] Riya: we're planning 1 hour at steady 3x peak with a 10 minute ramp and 10 minute cool-down. we'll capture full metrics and send a zip of traces.
[08:59] Priya: and what do you need from us before that?
[09:02] Jordan: confirm your gateway can set the token-length header and adjust client timeout to 30s; mark to confirm LB settings; riy a to push tuned-config.
[09:12] Mark: will confirm timeouts today.
[09:14] Riya: i'll drop tuned-config.yaml and a short runbook with the priority lane example.
[09:20] Jordan: ok let's do a quick wrap — next sync same time next week? or sooner after stress run?
[09:26] Sara: sooner please — we'll book a 30 minute follow-up the morning after the stress test.
[09:30] Jordan: perfect. thanks everyone.
